extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in the aesthetics of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the features that practitioners and commentators cite as making mathematical results, equations, proofs or notations 'beautiful' (e.g., elegance, surprise, economy, depth, connectedness). Useful for explaining or assessing aesthetic judgments about mathematics to lay and specialist audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'thrilling conceptual elegance' of a result: an aesthetic quality where the idea is neat, well-formed and intellectually satisfying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alex Bellos describes mathematical beauty as 'the thrilling conceptual elegance' and notes this often involves surprise, economy, depth, relevance and power. Examples cited as embodying conceptual elegance include Euler's identity and the Pythagorean theorem. Devlin likens Euler’s identity to a Shakespearean sonnet; Zeki's study links the experience to activity in the brain's pleasure/reward centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise / unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: An element of surprise or unexpected connection in a solution or theorem that yields aesthetic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights surprise as a component of elegance — e.g., Gauss’s rapid pairing trick (1+100, 2+99 ...) which is 'far more cunning' than the obvious slow method. Zeki's study and commentators emphasize that connecting previously unconnected elements often produces a feeling of wonder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy / concision / efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions, notations or arguments that achieve much with little — concise, economical expressions or methods are judged beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gauss’s paired-sum trick (fast, economical), Arabic numerals (more compact, immediate understanding compared with Roman numerals), and the article's reference to 'elegant concision'. Economy is explicitly listed among the elements that contribute to beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth (hidden richness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that reveals deep structure or layers of meaning — ideas whose beauty grows as one uncovers hidden depths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ramanujan's formulas are given as examples whose beauty may be 'acquired' as mathematicians discover hidden depths; Zeki & commentators note depth as a distinct aesthetic factor. Guidance: a result may look obscure at first but gain beauty as its deeper connections are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance / impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a theorem, formula or notation is relevant, useful, or has wide-ranging consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bellos lists 'relevance' and 'power' as parts of conceptual elegance. The article uses 'power' and 'relevance' to indicate that applicability and explanatory reach contribute to aesthetic value (e.g., Pythagoras's theorem is 'so powerful' as well as simple).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power / unifying force
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of a formula or theorem to solve many problems, unify disparate phenomena, or reveal broad principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euler’s identity unites several fundamental constants; the Index Theorem and the Ree Group Formula were chosen as beautiful partly for their deep mathematical significance. The article stresses that connecting elements that seemed unconnectable is central to perceived beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity paired with effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciation of solutions that are both simple in form and powerful in consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pythagoras’s theorem is singled out as 'beautiful because it is so simple, and so powerful.' Guidance: simple statements or formulas that nevertheless have broad utility are highly prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual / pattern aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Attractive visual patterns or easily visualised structures that are pleasing in appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alex Bellos curates 'colour-your-own mathematical patterns' chosen for their attractive appearance; the Metropolitan Museum of Art displayed mathematical expressions as framed art. Visual beauty (patterns, symmetry, form) is distinct from conceptual beauty but contributes to aesthetic judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation elegance and usability
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegance and efficiency of the symbolic or notational system used to express mathematical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses Arabic numerals as an example of a 'beautiful idea' because the notation is elegant, efficient and gives 'instant understanding' by length. Guidance: notation that reduces cognitive load and clarifies structure is aesthetically valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional / aesthetic response (neural correlate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective experience of beauty — a pleasurable, emotional response similar to responses to art or music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UCL neurobiologist Semir Zeki's study found that self-reported mathematical beauty in mathematicians correlated with activity in the medial orbito-frontal cortex, the same brain area active when people experience beauty from art or music; intensity of brain activity correlated with reported aesthetic intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity and plurality of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that judgments of mathematical beauty are subjective; different mathematicians will favor different formulas or styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that different professors chose different 'most beautiful' formulas; Erdős suggested beauty cannot be easily explained to someone who doesn't see it. Example contrasts: Euler’s identity and Pythagoras rated highly by many, while Ramanujan’s series and Riemann’s functional equation were rated ugly by some participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / expertise required
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciation of mathematical beauty often requires domain knowledge; deep aesthetic judgements may be inaccessible to laypeople.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commentators emphasize a technical barrier: many forms of mathematical beauty are 'acquired taste' and require reading or learning to appreciate. Vicky Neale notes one cannot assess beauty of an equation without 'quite a deep understanding' of the ideas it records. Guidance: translation/exposition can help lay audiences appreciate mathematical aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craftsmanship / elegance of argument (proof as performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty found in the manner of reasoning — proofs or solutions that unfold like a crafted performance (e.g., grandmaster chess analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ian Stewart compares reading a great mathematician to watching a grandmaster at chess or a craftsman at work: elegant unfolding and effective climax. Gauss's clever solution and other 'craftsman' performances are presented as sources of aesthetic pleasure.
